books.section: American Involvement in Vietnam, World War II–1963

primary_sources: Pentagon Papers, leaked by Daniel Ellsberg, 1971 (public record)

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from the grounding books' account of the Pentagon Papers

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Pentagon Papers, 1971, from the grounding books.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the Pentagon Papers. In 1971, newspapers published the Pentagon Papers, a secret Defense Department study of American involvement in Vietnam. The study showed a pattern of official deception: leaders had told the public the war was going well while their own reports said otherwise. Daniel Ellsberg, a Pentagon official, had leaked the study to the press.

stem: The Pentagon Papers most directly deepened public distrust of the government because they showed which of the following?

options.text: That the war had been won in secret while the public heard it was lost
options.misconception: The study showed the opposite: leaders said the war was going well while their own reports said otherwise.

options.text: That leaders told the public the war was going well while their reports said otherwise
That the newspapers had invented the war to sell more copies to readers
options.misconception: The war was real and the study was a government document; the newspapers published it, they did not invent it.

options.text: That Daniel Ellsberg had written the study to support the war effort
options.misconception: Ellsberg leaked the study because he opposed the war's direction; he did not write it to support the war.

rationales.A: The study showed leaders saying the war was going well while their own reports said otherwise, the reverse of this option.
rationales.B: The passage states the pattern directly: public claims that the war was going well against private reports saying otherwise.
rationales.C: The study was a secret Defense Department document, and the war was real; the newspapers published the study, they did not invent the war.
rationales.D: Ellsberg leaked the study to the press because he opposed the war's direction; he did not write it to support the war.
rationales.general:
1. The passage names the document: a secret Defense Department study of American involvement in Vietnam.
2. It then names the pattern inside it: official deception about how the war was going.
3. Background: leaders told the public the war was going well while their own reports said otherwise.
4. A public that learns it was told one story while officials held another stops trusting the storytellers.
Remember: A leak hurts trust when it shows two stories, one public and one private.
